zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, supplied package subset; CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the diplomatic text.

runs.text: coração atreiçoado contra alguem pera o ma-

lines.note: Continues f231's restored Gaixin example: harboring a treacherous heart against someone in order to kill him. Coração is body text here, although it also appeared as the preceding page's catchword.
Tar completes matar and finishes the cross-page description of murderous intention. The short continuation is a genuine body row.

Gajen is given an adverbial use meaning suddenly. The print appears to read xire rather than the contextually expected xite; the supplied reading is retained as a possible printed anomaly, not silently repaired from Japanese grammar.
Repente completes De-repente, 'suddenly'. The division is physical and is not joined in the transcription.
Gajimeqi concerns the sound made by insufficiently cooked things when chewed. Co begins cozidas; no hyphen is visible at this edge.

runs.text: zidas quandoſe mastigão como inhames mal co

lines.note: Completes cozidas and specifies chewing, with undercooked yams as the example. The printed quandoſe remains joined, and the second co again continues without a supplied hyphen.
Completes cozidos, agreeing with the yams named above. This ends the sound-description, not a separate cooking instruction.
Gajut names a particular medicine or medicinal substance. The bare terminal t is retained, and the gloss does not justify assigning a modern species.

runs.text: Hũas eruas que nacem nagoa de que ſe

lines.note: Gama denotes plants growing in water that are used for manufactured objects. The historical nagoa and the tilde in Hũas are copied as printed.
The plants are made into hats, mats and similar objects. This material-use description continues Gama; the provisional st form in esteiras is preserved.

runs.text: Certa laya de eſteiras feitas deſ

lines.note: Gamamushiro is a kind of mat made from the preceding plants. The scan supports Gamamuxiro, not OCR Gamunuxiro; deſ continues into deſtas without an invented hyphen.
Tas completes deſtas, 'these plants', explicitly referring back to Gama. The demonstrative links the mat entry to its material.
Gaman is here presumption or pride, paraphrased by ware manzuru. It must not be assigned only the familiar modern endurance sense.
Soberba completes the pride gloss. The example starts gaman no kokoro wo oko- and the printed hyphen is retained.
Su completes okosu: developing a proud disposition, translated as presuming greatly or becoming arrogant. The repeated historical enſoberbecerſe is not modernized.

runs.text: Esta palaura com outras junta ſigni-

lines.note: Gamaxij is explained as a form used in combination with other words. Signi- begins the Portuguese explanation of what the combination signifies.

runs.text: fica dar moſtra dalgũa couſa que não conuem.

lines.note: Completes significa: displaying some quality inappropriately. The scan clearly gives que, not OCR aue; the tilde in dalgũa is retained over u.
The example introduces a concessive phrase about speaking as though very discerning or knowledgeable. The spacing of mǒxi gotonaredomo is copied rather than resegmented into modern Japanese words.

runs.text: Posto que pareça moſtrarme muito ſabedor, ou

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the concession: 'although I seem to show myself very knowledgeable, or...'. The final alternative continues below.

runs.text: entendido no que digo, toda via, &c.

lines.note: Completes the claim to understanding what one says and adds 'nevertheless'. The printed two-word toda via is not normalized to modern todavia.
Gamocu is a cash or coin term, equated with Ieni. Gano me is the printed Japanese explanation; caixas is interpreted in this monetary context rather than as boxes.
Gamot denotes one's own possession, explained by waga mono. The final t is retained without adding a vowel.
Minha completes the alternative 'a thing of my own'. This short word finishes Gamot's possessive gloss.
Gan is equated with kari and glossed as a wild waterfowl. The Portuguese pato brauo is preserved rather than silently replaced with a modern zoological identification.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de tumba em que metem o

lines.note: This separate Gan is a kind of coffin or funerary receptacle. The final headword letter is n, not OCR u; its meaning is unrelated to the preceding bird entry.
The receptacle holds the dead body. This completes the funerary sense of Gan.

runs.text: O quem me dera, ou tiuera, oxala, &c.

lines.note: Gana expresses a wish, approximated by 'oh that I had' or 'would that'. The historical spellings and the lack of a supplied accent on O are preserved.

runs.text: Ajuntaſe ſempre a nomes, ou verbos.

lines.note: The dictionary says Gana always joins nouns or verbs. This is a grammatical usage note, not a new lexical entry.
Ganca denotes the area below the chin, explained by otogai no shita. The Portuguese paraphrase continues below rather than naming an independent object.
Completes 'under the chin/beard'. Together with the Japanese paraphrase it identifies the anatomical location of Ganca.
Ganchu means within the eyes. Manako no uchi supplies the same relation; the abbreviated Dẽtro retains its tilde.
Gancut is a rock cave or hollow, explained with iwa and ana. The printed bare final t is retained rather than expanded to a modern syllable.

Gangan concerns faces, with the repeated kao paraphrase and rosto. The example starts with abbreviated Gã-; the short terminal mark is retained as the supplied hyphen, although its exact outline remains faint.

Gan completes Gangan and the attached aitaiſu expresses meeting face to face. The printed sequence is kept joined rather than inserting an editorial boundary; the supplied st/ſt forms in the Portuguese are retained for the separate specialist typography review.
Gangin is a speck in the eye, paraphrased as manako no chiri. O- begins olhos and carries a visible hyphen.
The opening completes olhos, and gangin wo harau is removing the speck. The Portuguese ar- continues into argueiro below.
Completes argueiro dos olhos, the foreign particle in the eyes. This finishes the removal example.
Gangio denotes strength for work and walking. The printed circumflex is retained, and the list continues on the following row.
The example gangiona mono means a person with the physical strength just described. The Portuguese 'a man of...' continues below.
Specifies strength for labor, completing the characterization of the person. No additional Japanese headword begins here.
Gangio waza is work requiring strength. The phrase is a separate printed entry line and is not merged into the preceding example.
Braço adds the requirement for a strong arm or physical exertion. It completes the description of demanding work.
Ganjen means before one's eyes. The printed headword abbreviates n with a tilde over a; it is therefore Gãjen, not unmarked OCR Gajen or an editorially expanded Ganjen.
The sense extends to something evident. Kore ganjen de gozaru states that this is obvious; the printed ganjẽ preserves its abbreviated n.
The Portuguese says this is clear and manifest. Item introduces another sense and Gan- begins its repeated Japanese headword; the scan supports the supplied lowercase initial in isto.
Jen completes Ganjen, now glossed as a relative or close associate. X. is the upright regional label and is outside the italic Portuguese gloss.
Ganjenna denotes something clear and manifest, returning to the evidentness sense. The supplied st spelling in manifesta is retained without a global ligature reassignment.
Ganjenni is the corresponding adverb. The scan contains only the headword and Adu. on this final row; the OCR's ada- is not a genuine broken word, and no missing gloss is invented.
Ganjeqi is a rocky mass or crag, paraphrased by iwao and ishi. The initial I in Iuauo and the p of penedia correct OCR l and g confusions.
Ganmoku means eyes, with manako and me as Japanese equivalents. Both synonyms stay upright and are not marked as terms embedded in Portuguese.

runs.text: Nome de certa porta na China.

lines.note: Ganmon is the name of a particular gate in China. The gloss does not provide enough information to assign a more specific modern location, so none is supplied.
This Ganpi is a red flower and, by extension, its plant. Hũa retains the abbreviation mark and Item starts the botanical extension.
Completes the second sense: the plant that bears the red flower. The printed grave in dà is retained.
This separate Ganpi is a kind of paper, categorized as torinoko no rui. The paper sense is distinct from the preceding flower despite the identical headword.

Pel completes papel. Torinoco is a Japanese paper-name within the Portuguese definition; comparison with roman Torinocono above confirms that this occurrence is printed italic. It is marked for optional whole-word typeface review without imposing a font change.
Ganqe denotes an eye disease, paraphrased by me no wazurai. The Portuguese reads olhos, not OCR obos; the l and h are present despite their close contact.
Ganqen is the act of seeing with the eyes. The Japanese explanatory phrase is retained in its printed order rather than recast as modern syntax.
Ganqi encompasses sentient living beings. Vt introduces a class-expression on the next row and belongs to the italic gloss.
Ganqi no tagui refers to a kind or class of living creatures. The diminutive animalinhos begins the Portuguese illustration.
Adds small creatures or insects as an alternative explanation. It completes the Ganqi example rather than adding another headword.
Gankwo denotes the light or brightness of the eyes, explained by manako no hikari. The Portuguese is Claridade, with no extra u as in the OCR.
Resplandor adds radiance or shining of the eyes. This completes the brightness gloss of Ganquǒ.
Ganri means inside the eye, paraphrased by manako no uchi. The following proverbial example illustrates this interior location.
The example places a speck inside the eye and describes the world as narrow or small. The printed ſuboxi is retained rather than replaced with a more familiar modern adjective.

runs.text: Auendo argueiro nos olhos o mundo parece pe-

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the image: with a speck in the eyes the world appears small. Pe- is the visible beginning of pequeno.

runs.text: queno. i, Tudo parece conforme ao afeito que

lines.note: Completes pequeno and begins the moral explanation: everything appears according to one's disposition. Historical afeito is preserved rather than normalized from modern affect-related vocabulary.
The relevant disposition is what one has in the heart. This closes the figurative interpretation of the speck-in-the-eye example.
Ganryoku is the strength of the eyes, paraphrased by manako no chikara. The Portuguese alternative continues as vigor below.
The gloss identifies visual power. The example begins ganryoku ichidan, with no secure final point after ichidan; the sentence continues into qiyoxi below.
Qiyoxi completes the statement about exceptionally clear or strong eyesight. The Portuguese translates it as having very good sight.
Ganriki is assigned the same meaning as Ganriocu: strength of eyesight. The variant headword remains a separate entry.
Ganrui denotes a tear, paraphrased by manako no namida. The Portuguese construction continues with the organ from which it comes.
Olhos completes 'a tear of the eyes'. This is a short continuation of Ganrui.
Gansat denotes a letter and is equated with fumi. The scan supports Ganſat rather than OCR Ganiſat; the honorific Goganſat starts the following example.
The example says 'I received your letter'. Carta has t rather than OCR i; S. is the upright written-register label outside the italic translation.

This Gansǒ denotes the shape or appearance of the eyes, explained by manako no katachi. The mark over final o is abraded; the supplied caron is retained after reinspection. Fei continues into feição without an added hyphen.
Completes feição dos olhos, the configuration or appearance of the eyes. The line belongs to the preceding Gansǒ entry.
The second Ganso denotes plants of rocky shores, paraphrased by kishi no kusa. It is distinct from the eye-shape homograph above.
The plants grow on the rocky margin of the sea or a river. This completes the habitat description without imposing a species identification.
Gantǒ is a cave or rock hollow. The initial is G, not OCR C; iwa and hora explain the rocky cavity.
This Ganxei denotes the pupil of the eye, explained by manako hitomi. The historical Portuguese Minina is retained rather than normalized to menina.
The second Ganxei denotes the eyes' vigor, with manako no seiriki as the paraphrase. Vi- begins the Portuguese vigor.
Completes the strength gloss and supplies an example in which visual power has been exhausted. Tçuqita is kept with its printed tç sequence.

runs.text: Ter perdido a viſta, ou o vigor da viſta.

lines.note: The Portuguese interprets the example as losing sight or the strength of sight. Both alternatives are retained rather than reducing it solely to blindness.
The alternative predicates describe eyesight as strong or weak. The Latin l separates the alternatives and is not a Japanese particle.

runs.text: viſta boa, ou fraca dos olhos.

lines.note: Completes the translation: the eyes' sight is good or weak. This finishes the strong/weak example.
This Ganxǒ means on top of a rocky mass, explained by iwao no ue. The line ends with a comma, not the baseline's full stop, before the alternative below.
Adds 'or crag' to the rock-top location. The phrase is a continuation of the first Ganxǒ entry.
The second Ganxǒ means above the eyes, with manako no ue supplying the distinct Japanese explanation. The two homographs must remain separate.
Ganxo means a letter and is restricted by the written-register label S. The headword has no supplied long-o mark, and the label is upright.
This Ganxoku concerns facial appearance or color, expressed by kaobase iro. The Portuguese explanation continues on the next row.
Completes 'color of the face' and gives the example of containing a smile in one's expression. The printed spacing and long-s forms remain unchanged.

runs.text: Ter alegria, ou moſtrala no roſto. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese describes having joy or showing it in the face. Gã- begins the next example, retaining the abbreviated n and visible dividing mark.
Completes Ganxocuga cauaru, a change in facial color. The Portuguese explicitly confirms that the face changes color.

This separate Ganxocu concerns the look of the eyes, paraphrased by manako iro. The scan gives Ganxocu and iro, not OCR Canxocu and italicized ito; its Portuguese continuation was omitted from the baseline.

The restored final body row completes geito dos olhos, the look or expression of the eyes. Gan- at the far right is a separate catchword anticipating Ganyei on f233, not a second part of this sentence.
